# The Block Problem: Why GEO Content Needs Self-Contained Sections That Traditional SEO Ignores

## Introduction

We’re in the middle of a quiet tectonic shift in how content gets discovered: search used to be a “page game” — optimize the page, earn links, climb search engine rankings, and collect clicks. That world still exists, but it’s no longer sufficient. Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) forces a new requirement on content creators and engineers: content must be broken into self-contained, independently useful blocks that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems and embedding-based models can find, extract, and cite. I call this the “Block Problem.”

Why does this matter now? Because LLM-powered agents and generative search over vector indexes don’t treat a page as a single unit. They evaluate smaller chunks, embed them, and retrieve the bits that best answer a user’s prompt. When those chunks are independently coherent and citable, they’re far more likely to be surfaced as evidence in AI answers. When they’re not, the page’s overall SEO authority may be ignored or under-utilized. The consequences are both strategic and financial: AI-driven traffic converts differently (and often better), but traditional SEO metrics don’t capture this shift.

This post is a technical analysis for GEO practitioners. I’ll unpack the Block Problem, show how content chunking interacts with embeddings and RAG, present the empirical data that should make your team pay attention right now, and — most importantly — give you concrete, operational ways to restructure content so it’s AI-readable and citation-ready. You’ll also get a realistic look at current challenges: lack of standardization, measuring AI visibility, and how to coordinate SEO, PR, and content operations. If you’re building content for discovery in 2025 and beyond, this is no longer optional. It’s core architecture.

## Understanding the Block Problem

At its simplest: the Block Problem is the mismatch between page-centered traditional SEO and chunk-centered retrieval used by generative engines. Traditional SEO evolved around ranking signals — backlinks, domain authority, keywords across whole pages, and SERP features. GEO is built around retrieval models, embeddings, and RAG systems that assess relevance at the block level. That inversion creates three fundamental tensions.

1) Retrieval models replace ranking algorithms. LLMs and vector search don’t “crawl and rank” exactly the way Google’s algorithm historically did. Instead, content is tokenized, chunked, and embedded into high-dimensional vector space. A user’s prompt is embedded and matched against the closest vectors. The retrieved blocks are then used to generate or ground a response. That means a single high-authority page with mixed topics won’t necessarily surface if its useful content is buried in an unstructured paragraph. Conversely, a short, well-structured 250-word block can become the primary citation for an AI answer.

2) Answers over clicks. AI-driven interfaces increasingly provide complete answers inline, often reducing click-throughs. Recent industry observations show that AI Overviews appear in 16% of U.S. searches, more than double rates from earlier in 2025; when these overviews show, they can reduce website clicks by around 34.5%. The net effect is more zero-click information retrieval, especially for informational queries. But while clicks drop, conversion quality often rises: AI search traffic converts at roughly 4.4x the rate of traditional organic search — meaning fewer clicks, but higher commercial intent and better downstream results when those clicks happen.

3) Fragment-level authority emerges. Think of “position zero 2.0”: instead of a page-based featured snippet, brands now compete to be the cited fragment within an LLM response. LLMs and generative engines do not cite entire pages; they cite the specific chunks used to assemble the answer. That means your brand’s visibility in AI results depends on whether discrete blocks are structured to be independently useful and verifiable.

These dynamics are not hypothetical. The market is moving rapidly: the AI marketing industry expanded to $20.4 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach about $82.2 billion by 2030 (roughly a 25% CAGR). Search-specific GenAI ad spending is expected to accelerate, with certain forecasts noting it may roughly double between 2025 and 2026 and exceed $25 billion by 2029. Meanwhile, Gartner predicts traditional search engine volume could shrink by about 25% by 2026 as discovery fragments into AI-driven modes. ChatGPT and similar agents process extraordinary volumes (ChatGPT alone handling approximately 2.5 billion prompts daily), driving adoption of retrieval-first approaches across enterprise and consumer use cases.

The Block Problem arises because content teams have been trained to optimize for page-level metrics. GEO demands a rethinking: design content so that each 200–300-word chunk (the practical size many teams now use) can be retrieved, attributed, and consumed without relying on surrounding context.

## Key Components and Analysis

Let’s dig into the technical components that make block-first architecture work — and why each matters for discoverability by generative engines.

Chunking & Chunk Size
- How: Break content into discrete units (200–300 words recommended by current best practice). Each chunk should have a clear header, answer a single question or subtopic, and include at least one verifiable data point or claim.
- Why: Embedding models compute similarity at the vector level. Shorter, tightly topical chunks yield more precise embeddings and reduce noise. A 2,000-word page that covers five topics will produce vectors that mix topics; a 250-word block produces a vector closely aligned with a single concept, increasing retrieval precision.

Embeddings & Vector Indexing
- How: Index each chunk’s text into a vector store (Pinecone, Milvus, FAISS, etc.) and maintain metadata: URL, header, publication date, author, and a short excerpt for citation.
- Why: Retrieval engines use vector similarity to pull candidate blocks. Metadata helps the RAG orchestration layer pick content for answer grounding — and is essential for generating proper citations and for downstream measurement.

RAG Orchestration & Prompt Engineering
- How: Build your retrieval pipeline to prefer recent, well-sourced, and metadata-rich chunks. Use filters for recency and domain trust. In the generation step, favor blocks with explicit data points and clear citations.
- Why: LLMs are good at blending retrieved text into coherent answers, but they’re biased toward cleaner, shorter supporting blocks. Orchestration that surfaces stable, factual chunks reduces hallucination and increases the chance your content is cited verbatim.

Citation-Friendly Content Patterns
- How: Use direct-answer patterns (question — one-line answer — short expansion), bullet facts, and numbered steps. Where possible, include precise figures, dates, or named entities and attach schema markup that labels the block’s type (FAQ, how-to, definition).
- Why: LLMs prefer content they can copy from directly. Precise, verifiable statements are more likely to be presented as evidence and attributed.

Recency & Refresh Cadence
- How: Schedule content refreshes for high-value blocks and add versioning metadata. Surface a “last updated” tag in each chunk’s metadata.
- Why: Recent content is favored in many retrieval systems. Teams that refresh and re-index often see better retrieval frequency. In practice, page refresh is a distinct GEO lever that differs from traditional SEO refresh tactics.

Measurement & Attribution
- How: Track AI citation frequency, name-mention attribution in generated answers, conversion metrics for AI traffic, and compare those to traditional SERP performance.
- Why: Traditional SEO KPIs (rankings, organic clicks) no longer tell the whole story. Broworks reported that after implementing GEO best practices, 10% of organic visits came from generative engines within 90 days and 27% of that traffic converted to Sales-Qualified Leads — and visitors from LLMs stayed about 30% longer. Those are the kinds of business signals teams should measure.

Operational Alignment
- How: Create cross-functional workflows: content architects who design blocks, developers who handle indexing, SEO specialists who map keyword-to-block, and PR/comm teams who manage reputation signals.
- Why: GEO is multi-disciplinary. The block is the cross-over unit where content, technical SEO, schema, and PR meet. Without alignment, content teams will revert to page-level templates that don’t serve retrieval systems.

Collectively, these components describe why self-contained blocks are not a cosmetic change: they’re a new content data model that maps content atoms (blocks) to retrieval systems and then to generative pipelines.

## Practical Applications

If you’re convinced the Block Problem matters, here are practical ways to implement block-first content strategies that produce measurable GEO outcomes.

Design Templates for Atomic Blocks
- Template: Header (question format), 1–2 sentence answer (concise, citation-ready), 2–3 supporting bullets with data or examples, and metadata fields (source, last updated, author).
- Execution: Convert existing long-form pages into a series of these blocks and re-index them individually. Use internal anchors and stable URIs for each block to enable precise citation.

Rebuild Topic Clusters as Block Graphs
- Template: Treat a topic cluster not as a pillar page but as a graph of interconnected blocks. Each block covers a subtopic and links (and references) neighboring blocks. Maintain an index page that aggregates linked blocks for humans while keeping each block independently retrievable for machines.

Implement a Block-Level Metadata Layer
- What to store: URL, block-id, header, canonical page, schema type (FAQ, step, definition, data point), last-updated timestamp, and short excerpt.
- Why: This metadata is what retrieval orchestration needs to filter candidates. It also supports accountability and auditing for attribution.

Automate Chunking & Ingest Pipelines
- Tools: Use content processing scripts to detect headings and break content into 200–300-word segments. Automate embedding generation and push to vector indexes on publish/update.
- Benefits: Eliminates manual friction and ensures your vector store represents live site content.

Adapt Content Operations for Frequency
- Strategy: Prioritize refresh cycles on high-value blocks. Treat them like ad creative: test variations of phrasing and measure which receives more citations and conversions.
- Impact: Recency matters. Many retrieval systems prioritize fresh, factually accurate content.

Measure GEO-Specific KPIs
- Track: citation count in LLM outputs, named-brand mentions in AI answers, conversion rate from generative engine traffic, dwell time, and block-level retrieval frequency.
- Example: Broworks’ early GEO program produced a 10% share of organic visits from generative engines within 90 days; 27% of that traffic became Sales-Qualified Leads. Those are the right kinds of outcome-level KPIs.

Coordinate PR and Reputation Signals
- How: Integrate PR reach with block strategy. Press mentions and authoritative references increase the trust score of discrete blocks, which helps retrieval engines prefer them.
- Why: GEO is not just content engineering; it’s reputation engineering. The block that’s quoted across high-authority domains is more likely to be retrieved.

These practical steps move teams from theory to execution. The consistent theme: make each block independently useful, verifiable, and discoverable.

## Challenges and Solutions

Adopting block-first GEO practices is powerful, but it’s not without friction. Here are the major challenges you’ll face and practical mitigations.

Challenge: No Industry Standard
- Problem: Unlike traditional SEO’s decades of Google-focused guidelines, GEO lacks a central rulebook. Teams must experiment.
- Solution: Build empirically. Start with the de facto standard (200–300 word chunks, clear headers, citation-ready one-line answers). Instrument everything to learn which blocks get retrieved and cited. Create internal playbooks and share findings across the organization.

Challenge: Measurement Complexity
- Problem: Existing analytics were built for page-level measurement. AI visibility (citations in LLM answers) is a different signal.
- Solution: Invest in tooling to monitor AI outputs, capture when LLMs cite your content, and correlate those events with downstream conversions. Use webhook-based tracking for click-throughs from agents that provide follow links and UTM parameters for attributed visits.

Challenge: Content Volume vs. Quality
- Problem: Chunking increases the number of indexing units dramatically, which can lead to thin or repetitive blocks.
- Solution: Enforce editorial quality gates for blocks. Each block must be independently useful and fact-checked. Consolidate redundant blocks and use canonicalization metadata to avoid dilution.

Challenge: Organizational Change
- Problem: Content teams, SEO, PR, and engineering operate in silos.
- Solution: Establish a GEO working group with representatives from content, SEO, engineering, and PR. Create SLAs for block publishing, embedding generation, and re-indexing. Treat block design as a product with KPIs.

Challenge: Risk of Misattribution & Hallucination
- Problem: LLMs can still hallucinate or misattribute if the retrieval set is noisy.
- Solution: Ensure blocks include verifiable data points and links to primary sources. On the RAG side, prefer high-trust domains and apply confidence thresholds; if low confidence, do not present a citation.

Challenge: Resource Allocation
- Problem: Implementing RAG pipelines, vector stores, and indexing pipelines requires engineering resources.
- Solution: Start with hybrid approaches: manually curate high-value pages into blocks and use managed vector services or SaaS GEO platforms to lower engineering overhead. Prioritize use cases with high commercial impact first.

Each challenge has an operational path forward. The common denominator: treat GEO as a product and measure it the same way you would any product launch — with hypotheses, experiments, and iterative improvements.

## Future Outlook

If you’re planning for the next 12–24 months, here are realistic expectations and strategic bets grounded in current trends.

Search will fragment but not disappear. Gartner’s projection of a potential 25% decline in traditional search volume by 2026 doesn’t mean Google or traditional engines vanish; it means discovery will be distributed across agent-based interfaces, platform-specific assistants, and generative overviews that reduce clicks for many informational queries. Expect your organic funnel to shift. The “crocodile mouth” effect—impressions up, clicks down—is real: average website search traffic reportedly dropped about 21% over the past year, and AI Overviews already reduce clicks substantially when present. That’s structural.

Citation-driven visibility will become a primary channel. Brands that secure frequent, high-quality citations inside LLM answers will gain a new form of top-of-funnel advantage. Today’s “position zero 2.0” is fragment-level: being the block an LLM quotes. As consumers increasingly rely on AI for recommendations — reports show 58% now use AI for product recommendations, versus 25% two years earlier — the stakes for being an attributable, trusted block are clear.

Economics will shift toward outcome-based models. Results-as-a-Service (RaaS) for GEO is emerging; clients want measurable business impact from GEO investments. Early GEO adopters report strong conversion quality from AI-driven traffic. For example, Broworks’ GEO work led to 10% of organic visits from generative engines within 90 days and a 27% conversion to Sales-Qualified Leads from that subset. That’s the kind of ROI that will make GEO budgets defensible.

Standards will emerge, but slowly. Expect consensus on chunk sizes, metadata best practices, and indexing cadences to solidify over the next 12–24 months. Early adopters who architect systems now will have long-term advantage, but the playing field will eventually standardize around practices like 200–300-word chunks with explicit metadata and refresh cycles.

Tooling and platforms will commoditize parts of the stack. Vector databases, managed RAG services, and GEO analytics platforms will make implementation more accessible. However, content strategy and editorial quality will remain the barriers to scale. Automation can densify your vector store, but it cannot replace human judgment for factual correctness and tone.

Cross-channel signals will matter. LLMs ingest signals from multiple sources. PR, social, and structured data (schema) will increasingly influence block-level trust. Coordinate external communications to elevate the authority of your blocks across the web.

In short: GEO becomes central to discovery strategy. The Block Problem is not a temporary nuisance — it’s a content architecture problem that will define winners and laggards in the era of generative discovery.

## Conclusion

The Block Problem forces a reframe: content is no longer a page-first asset; it’s a collection of block-level knowledge artifacts that must be independently useful, verifiable, and discoverable by retrieval systems. Traditional SEO gives you domain authority and pages that rank in SERPs—still valuable—but it won’t guarantee citation or prominence in an LLM-generated answer. GEO demands a different operational model: chunk content, enrich it with metadata, index blocks into vectors, orchestrate retrieval carefully, and measure citations and conversions rather than just ranks.

The market signals are stark. The AI marketing industry is expanding rapidly (from $20.4B in 2024 toward about $82.2B by 2030), GenAI ad spending is accelerating, and analysts predict meaningful declines in traditional search volume as AI interfaces proliferate. Empirical results already show the promise of GEO: Broworks’ early program delivered 10% of organic visits from generative engines in 90 days, with 27% converting to S.Q.L.s and LLM visitors staying about 30% longer. These aren’t abstract metrics — they’re business outcomes.

If you manage content, product, or digital strategy, your immediate task is to treat blocks as first-class units of work. Convert priority pages into 200–300-word self-contained sections, instrument your vector store and retrieval pipelines, and measure citation-based visibility alongside traditional SEO KPIs. GEO is multidisciplinary — it sits at the intersection of content, engineering, SEO, and PR — so build cross-functional processes and treat it like a product with iterative experiments and clear KPIs.

Actionable takeaways
- Break content into 200–300-word, question-focused blocks with clear headers.
- Add block-level metadata (schema type, last-updated, author, canonical page, excerpt).
- Index blocks into a managed vector store and automate embedding generation on publish/update.
- Prioritize refresh cadence for high-value blocks and track block retrieval frequency.
- Measure AI-specific KPIs: citation count, named-brand mentions, conversion rate from generative engine traffic.
- Align SEO, content, engineering, and PR; treat GEO as a product with SLAs and experiments.

The Block Problem is a design and operational problem, but it’s solvable. Teams that build block-first content systems now will win the new era of AI-driven discovery. Start converting pages into blocks today — your citations, conversions, and long-term visibility depend on it.
